n: Market abuse (insider dealing, wash trading, pump-and-dump) as a predicate and laundering vehicle
ds: Securities and token markets are manipulated or exploited with inside information to generate illicit profit, and the same trading channels are then used to disguise the source of other criminal funds by manufacturing apparent trading gains or losses. Typical vehicles are thinly traded issuers, newly listed tokens, linked or nominee accounts and coordinated promotion. The proceeds are quickly withdrawn, moved offshore or converted, so surveillance and AML teams need shared visibility of trading behaviour and money movement.

src.t: FATF, Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Securities Sector, 2009
European Union, Regulation (EU) No 596/2014 on market abuse (Market Abuse Regulation), 2014
FATF, Virtual Assets: Red Flag Indicators of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing, 2020

rat: Trading accounts and token venues; proceeds moved offshore or into virtual assets.

ind.n: Wash or matched trades between connected parties
ind.cx: Repeated buying and selling of the same instrument or token between connected accounts at no real change of beneficial ownership, creating false volume or a price trail that justifies deposits and withdrawals.
ind.fp: Collectors moving assets between own wallets.
ind.ds: Assets or securities are traded repeatedly between linked accounts or wallets at unrealistic prices.

ind.n: Trading in low-liquidity securities with unrelated parties
ind.cx: Concentrated dealing in thinly traded or micro-cap issuers where a few accounts can set the price and counterparties appear to be pre-arranged.
ind.ds: Illiquid instruments used to move value.

ind.n: Newly established customer with rapid high-value activity
ind.cx: Accounts opened and funded shortly before a promoted issuer or token moves, then used almost entirely to accumulate that one holding.
ind.fp: Genuine start-ups or fast-growing businesses can scale quickly; test against business plan and evidence of operations.
ind.ds: A recently formed customer with little history or track record quickly records large turnover or trades in high-value or restricted goods.

ind.n: Collusive purchases between related buyer and seller accounts
ind.cx: Related buyer and seller accounts on a trading venue, NFT marketplace or token exchange, linked by device, funding source or wallet, trade with each other to fabricate demand.
ind.ds: Accounts sharing devices or funding sources transact with each other to create revenue.

ind.n: Rapid movement offshore or to crypto after receipt
ind.cx: Sale proceeds from a spike in price are moved offshore or into virtual assets within days, before the price retraces or a regulator or venue intervenes.
ind.fp: Genuine international payments or planned crypto purchases by established customers.
ind.ds: Incoming funds are quickly sent abroad or converted to virtual assets soon after being credited.

ind.n: Shell entity with no operating footprint
ind.cx: The issuer or promoted company has no real operations, staff or revenue, so its securities have little value beyond the promotional narrative.
ind.fp: Start-ups, holding companies and special-purpose vehicles may legitimately lack a footprint.
ind.ds: Entity has no staff, premises, website or trading history consistent with its stated activity, yet receives significant payments.

ind.n: Trading ahead of material non-public announcements
ind.cx: Core insider-dealing signal, and a route for turning inside information into spendable proceeds that are then banked or moved.
ind.fp: Skilled analysis of public information, sector-wide positioning, scheduled portfolio rebalancing or pre-planned option exercises can look similar. Look for repeat timing and links to insiders.
ind.ds: A customer or linked accounts take unusually large or well-timed positions shortly before a price-sensitive event such as a takeover, results release or listing decision, then close out soon after the news.

ind.n: Promotion campaign alongside concentrated selling by connected holders
ind.cx: Defines the pump-and-dump pattern and links the promoters to the beneficiaries of the exit trades.
ind.fp: Genuine news, index inclusion or legitimate investor-relations activity can raise interest and volume. Weight the link between promoters and sellers.
ind.ds: Coordinated social-media, messaging-group or cold-call promotion of a low-priced instrument coincides with unusual buying volume while a small group of connected holders sells into the rise.

ind.n: Orders placed and cancelled without intent to execute
ind.cx: Manipulative price-formation behaviour that precedes a profitable trade and is only visible in order-level data.
ind.fp: Market makers and algorithmic strategies legitimately cancel at high rates. Compare to the customer's stated strategy and the benefit on related positions.
ind.ds: Large orders are repeatedly entered and withdrawn before execution, or small orders are layered, in a way that moves the visible price or depth in favour of positions held elsewhere.

ind.n: Token deployer or insider wallets distributing holdings into promoted price rise
ind.cx: Crypto equivalent of insiders selling into a pump, including rug-pull style exits.
ind.fp: Vesting schedules, treasury management and disclosed team allocations can involve similar transfers. Check against published token schedules.
ind.ds: Wallets linked to a token's creator, early allocation or liquidity pool move large balances to exchanges or fresh wallets as promotion drives the price up, often followed by liquidity removal.

ctl.ds: Detects funds that return to their origin or loop between linked parties through reciprocal, matched, netted or round-trip flows using graph analysis and account comparison. It exposes artificial turnover and loan-back structures.
Links accounts, devices, addresses, directors and beneficiaries to surface rings, shared attributes and flow structures that single-account views miss. It supports detection of organised networks.

Monitors specialised products such as insurance, securities, safe deposit and prepaid instruments for surrender, free delivery, overpayment, assignment, matched trades and unusual access. It catches product-specific abuse.

Compares actual activity with the customer's declared profile, history and peers and alerts on material or trend-breaking deviation, usually as a contextual signal. It catches change that rules on fixed thresholds miss.

ctl.n: Tightened monitoring for new accounts and entities
ctl.ds: Applies lower thresholds and closer review during the first months of an account or entity and alerts on turnover far above onboarding projections. It addresses the elevated risk at the start of a relationship.
Traces exposure of deposit and withdrawal addresses to illicit clusters and screens wallets with risk-scored alerts. It reveals on-chain exposure.
Clusters customers, vendors and entities that share addresses, phones, devices, officers or bank details, including against staff records. It reveals common control and hidden relationships.

Alerts on unusual countries, corridors, deposit locations and geolocation dispersion relative to the customer profile or on activity near designated risk regions. It focuses review on geographic anomalies.
Alerts when inflows are quickly moved out with little retained balance, including cash-in fast-out and rapid conversion or cash-out. It reveals accounts used as conduits for layering.
Rules that alert on abnormal count, value or speed of movements over defined windows compared with customer profile and peer norms. They provide baseline coverage across many typologies.

Runs continuous screening of customers, owners, introducers, suppliers and counterparties against curated news, leaks, regulatory notices and enforcement releases, with reliability grading and identity disambiguation. It surfaces negative information that registers and lists do not carry.

Tests whether an entity has real operations such as premises, staff, stock and contracts through documents, site or virtual visits, open-source footprint and shell-risk indicators. It helps identify shell and front companies with no genuine activity.

Requires declarations of conflicts from staff and third parties with annual refresh, rotation of relationship managers and challenge of exceptions. It reduces the chance that decisions are shaped by personal interest.

Translates published and sanitised typologies and red flags into targeted monitoring scenarios and context-aware rules that are reviewed periodically. It aligns monitoring with known criminal methods.

ctl.n: Counterparty VASP and platform due diligence
ctl.ds: Assesses the licensing, AML controls, jurisdiction and reputation of counterparty exchanges, over-the-counter desks and other virtual asset service providers before enabling flows, and reviews them periodically. It limits exposure through weak or complicit counterparties.
Flags direct and indirect exposure to mixers, privacy services and obfuscation tools against defined thresholds and applies enhanced review. It manages the traceability loss these tools create.
